doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: The sound of early jazz recordings
summary: He describes the vibrato, downbeat push and afterbeat of King Oliver and Armstrong records, and that friends did not share his taste.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Did you start listening to it and sort of analyzing what you were hearing? You know, what kind of — was it a string bass, was this a — you know, what’s the instrumentation here? When did that come about for you?

Well on the early jazz recordings that my grandmother had there was definitely this sound that instrumentalists produced in those days that was a lost language as far as the fifties were concerned, particularly the way the saxophones would have that kind of little vibrato, that little moan, either hearing King Oliver or Louis Armstrong or some of the novelty cornetists. They had that kind of, you know, agitated vibrato. And there was a definite push on the downbeat, to get the thing going, and then this afterbeat. So here’s this — I just took it all in, that this was something that I could not experience in my generation. It was something special about this music. And no one told me this, I found it and it was my music. I was just totally drawn to it.
Were you able to enlist any of your friends?
